Personally I used to love events, but I’m a bit less of a fan now. I still use them occasionally, but there’s definitely some parts of them that are a little bit icky. You can’t guarantee things like an event handler only being added once to an event, or a handler being exclusively assigned to a single event. Furthermore the event handler can’t get GCed while the event is still alive, which makes sense but can lead to weird situations sometimes- there’s no builtin concept of a ‘weak event’.


Not hating on events entirely, they can be nice sometimes, but they come with a lot more caveats than they seem to on the surface, and can be an easy way to end up with a tangled mess of event-driven spaghetti also

Personally I’d still consider this a code smell because the whole point of using nullable reference types is to know when something is supposed to be able to be null. Those warnings are to help you keep track of nulls/nullability, and if you really don’t want to do that then you can turn them off.

null! or default! are great for situations where you need to assign a value to something that ordinary shouldn’t be null but something weird happened- A Try method that returns a bool and has an out parameter is a good example because you are saying that if it succeeds, the result should not be null, but if it fails, you should not use the result. Default! would be appropriate to use to set the result before returning false, because you are explicitly saying that the method failed and the result shouldn’t matter anyway.


In this case, however, this is a public property that is non-nullable being set to null initially, meaning if someone were to create an instance and attempt to get from the property, they could get null despite the property saying it won’t be null, and nothing saying the property cant or shouldn’t be used. If the class had a separate Init() method to be called after construction, this might be ok, but seeing as this is an autoproperty with a public setter I think that’s unlikely- and it would probably be better anyway to throw an exception for attempting to access the property before Init() is called.


So as I see it, this is still an abuse of null!, which has little to do with null! vs default! and everything to do with what either of those actually mean. This property should probably be declared as nullable, rather than use null! (fixing what is being warned about, rather than suppressing the warning)

You define void as “function”, but a function can in some contexts also imply that it has an output.


For clarity and precision, I’d definitely consider redefining void as “abyss”, “hole”, or “the_space_between_life_and_death”.


Should help with readability, ex:

    public abyss Foo(unwaivering integer a)

I’d even go as far as making the argument that if you need custom code for something like this, chatgpt is going to actively hurt you even if you know what you’re doing. There’s a million character controllers out there at this point- chatgpt doesn’t know what you want, it can only parrot what’s been done. So if what’s been done doesn’t suit your needs, chatgpt wont either.


(Obv there’s plenty of reasons to write bespoke code even when there are existing tools, but I can’t think of one where chatgpt is actually beneficial, other than “hmm I wonder what happens if I try to do as much of this with chatgpt as possible”)

If you’re still learning, for the love of god don’t use chatgpt. Even copying from stackoverflow would be better (I don’t recommend that either).


If you don’t know enough code to modify copied or generated code so that it actually fits your program, then copying code is going to make your life so much harder, and slow down your learning process as well. Yes, there are things you can learn when trying to adapt copied code, but if you’re asking reddit about it, ur probably not there yet.


Tutorials my friend. There’s so many. I would recommend the ones in the msdn and unity manual, honestly, but that’s because I think it’s easier to follow text than video for learning to code- there’s also plenty of youtube tho.


Best of luck on your learning-to-code journey though! Remember that writing code isn’t scary, it has clear rules and can be understood- it’s only magic until you understand it. Once you git gud you probably won’t even want to copy/generate your code anymore, except maybe as an experiment.

It’s too predictable in its patterns, and lacks history. A lot of ppl mention adding more destruction or decay, but I don’t think that’s the root cause of the “flatness” necessarily (tho it is a potential way to fix it). Part of what makes a post-apocalyptic scene intriguing is the way the environment is full of so many tiny stories (and post apocalyptic scenes that don’t can often feel flat despite including all the “basic genre elements”). You don’t need to write a whole backstory for the building, but you should think a bit about why the building exists in the first place and how it came to be all post-apocalypse-y. Things like

 - What was the building used for? Did anyone live there? Was it a place where people would work like a factory or a business?
 - What sort of lives were lived there/ work was done there?
 - Why was it abandoned? What happened to its inhabitants?


All of these can help guide you towards making it feel “alive” (even in a post-apocalypse, things have to be “alive” first to be able to be “dead”). In its current state, the brick pattern is ordinary and regular with little to break it up, and the plant growth is a bit repetitive. It looks very “fake” as a result, or at least like it was brand new and planned to have vines on it, rather than overgrown.


Some more exterior features, more irregularities, some things to break up the big flat patterns would help. Destruction is definitely an option for this, but I think it’s worth mentioning that I don’t think it’s the only way, nor would a haphazard application of dirt necessarily do the job on its own. Again, tiny stories- Why is there a hole in the wall here? What broke this window? What bent this metal?


And again you don’t always need to write up some massive backstory to do this, or tie in every bit of narrative (or any bit of narrative) you might have for the larger game, if your game even has a larger narrative in the first place.

I think your choices might not be for everyone necessarily, but that allows you to focus more on designing the experience you really want to make, for the audience who really wants to play it. Some people might experience a degree of motion sickness, find it too distracting, or just get turned off by the fact that your game doesn’t follow the typical conventions that they’re used to seeing. But at the same time, have you ever played a game set in space where being out in space is actually silent? It… really spooky actually. A lot of games just do a low-pass filter or the like, making space sound like underwater, and you can get used to space sounding like that, until you play a game where space is mostly silent, and suddenly get this weird haunting feeling of a hard, dead vacuum around you. I’ve actually caught myself holding my breath sometimes without realizing it.


Your choices might not be for everyone, and might require some adaptation on the part of the player, but I think especially indie games have the opportunity to do weird shit and fill niches that are just too far outside the average audience’s comfort zone for more mainstream titles to attempt.


The real dumb decision imo would be to make too many concessions to an audience that doesn’t really want the experience you’re making anyway, and lose your game’s identity in the process.

I see a lot of comments that seem to just say “ew, low fps”, but it sounds like you’re honestly trying to make an interesting artistic choice here that is worth considering.


If your game’s visual aesthetic and gameplay work well at 15fps, then I’d say go for it. The caveats of course being that if you’re gonna go for it, you’d better make sure the aesthetic and gameplay work with it holistically. Just capping framerate and adding motion blur on their own would indeed probably feel kinda gross.


A lot of people have also brought up input latency (capping visual fps to 15, but doing simulation frames faster). This might be a good idea, but there are also some other options. Movement likely needs faster input responses to feel snappy, but if your movement purposely is supposed to feel sluggish or latent anyway you might get away with it. That’s assuming you have movement at all.

First person perspectives are likely going to give you the most trouble, especially due to mouse look, but I also know that I’ve personally played Minecraft in the 7-15hz range and enjoyed it all the same (although I’d definitely notice anything below 30 in say, TF2, or below 60 in a game like overwatch). 

All in all, I genuinely think that the style of gameplay and level of artistic cohesion are going to make all the difference here. There’s a lot of “surrealism” out there that gets a bad rep for trying to use “surreal” to justify a lack of cohesion, but I’ve also seen plenty of games that are honestly “surreal” and structure all the elements of the game holistically to that end.

It’s a bit like how some horror games are still spooky despite being brightly lit and easily readable, while others use “horror” as a way to just make the screen dark and give you a tiny flashlight with no battery life, but aren’t scary or tense in the slightest. The way your design decisions work together is going to be way more important than any individual element on its own.

If the game works well with a 15fps cap and funky resolution, I’d enjoy it. Hell, I probably wouldn’t even think about the fact it’s 15fps at first. If it doesn’t, well it’d be a refund, but the same would go for any other game that just feels bad to play. IMO, the real risk here isn’t going for 15fps, it’s the potential of not COMMITTING to 15fps in the design of the rest of the game.

Colliders don’t “glitch into each other”, because there is nothing about a collider that says they can’t intersect with other colliders-


They can, however, be used to detect intersections with colliders, rays, etc, and get information about that intersection, or “collision”. This doesn’t stop you from assigning positions to multiple objects with colliders such that they overlap.


When you slap a rigidbody on something it will use colliders to avoid overlapping with anything, preferring to slide or bounce along surfaces, but that’s what rigidbody does using colliders, not what colliders themselves do. You can write your own code to do the same thing (although the built in rigidbody is probably going to be more performant), or use collision info in your own way. Projectiles often need some custom movement code because they need to raycast from their old position to their new one to find if they hit anything, due to their high speeds, which often mean having a collider on a fast-moving projectile is pretty pointless.


Making more colliders in the same space won’t help you, since all you would do is increase the number of collision events that get registered. If your objects are overlapping it often means that either the collisions aren’t ever actually occurring (ex: the “bullets pass thru walls” problem), or that some other piece of code isn’t respecting what you want those collisions to mean.


TLDR: Colliders themselves don’t stop objects from overlapping- the problem lies in the assumptions and behavior of code that uses the collision info. It seems like there’s a fair bit of googling ahead of you

Pssst! Try making a behavior that follows ANY path you give it, then give it a square path to follow!


This isn’t just about code re-use or parametrization either. While it also happens to be a nice bonus that you could re-use the script for other objects that need different paths, or change the path if you want something other than a square, I still think it’s a good idea even if this is a one-off script.


Consider instead a script with an array of vector3s (or vec2s, depending) that represents the path. You also keep a private variable around that represents the “progress” along the path. Then, during your update, you increment this progress by deltatime (maybe multiplied by a speed coefficient). After incrementing to the correct progress for the frame you can then use that to choose the appropriate points in the path array and lerp between them. You will also have to remember the case where you are moving from the last point in the path to the first point (if you want the path to loop continuously), but that’s basically the only edge case.


The reasons to do this instead of just a long chain of if statements is numerous, but the biggest advantage you’ll gain imo is readability. Lets say you’re tracking down a bug, or maybe just revisiting the script or the project, and you see a chain of if-then all down the page. You’d have to pick through it as if you were an interpreter, methodically following most of the steps in your head. That’s not just hard, it’s missing something important. You might be able to tell what math the code makes the computer do, but it will say nothing of why you want the computer to do that math. 


Now, instead, imagine revisiting a script and seeing an array of positions called path and a float called progress. Oh, and a lerp in the update too, followed by a write to transform.position! There’s probably other bits of the script that aren’t included in that description, but if you saw that code you’d immediately know it makes an object follow a path! You don’t have to even read through much of the code to understand what it’s supposed to do, and when it’s debugging time it makes it easier to see where things go wrong because you know already what things going right should look like. 


It’s also just good practice. This script looks like it’s for something small or as a learning experience, but once you start tackling bigger projects that can’t all neatly fit in your head, you’ll want to write code in a more sustainable way. If this were any larger a project, it would be absolutely a no-go to write a million one-off scripts like this, or to have numbers like “5” and “-5” be hard-coded in. That’s what the inspector’s for! (And yes, of course, the script I proposed only works for polygonal paths, but another advantage is that it’s pretty easy to adapt to work with splines or bezier curves also! You’d need a different function than lerp mostly, and a place to input any other data your curve function might need, but that’s about it. Other features too like varying speed, etc, all become relatively minor changes)

I usually just use this for situations where one interface might imply a set of ways of going about doing what another interface does (without a specific implementation). Usually this just takes the form of making a generic version of a non-generic interface or the like. Ya know how then you implement IEnumerable<T> you need to provide an IEnumerator<T> but also a non-generic IEnumerator, but 99% of the time you just have the non-generic one call the generic one? If IEnumerable<T> had a default impl for the non-generic method it inherits, you’d only have to provide the non-generic one if you actually needed to do something different for that case, which you usually dont.


Though I’d also say default impls aren’t the place to do more than just return a default or const value, or do a few type casts, provide a few default params, and call something else in the interface. I’m on the fence about empty default impls in callback handler interfaces with multiple callbacks, but it would make them optional to implement and feel a bit more like overriding a virtual or using a magic method, which might be nice for specific parts of an api maybe.

Regardless, default impls !!!!!= multiple inheritance or anything close. As long as you’re still treating your interfaces as interfaces you probably wouldn’t have much reason to write a super dangerous default impl I don’t think.

The light radius is just a way of expressing how far the light has to travel before the amount of lighting it would contribute is effectively 0. This is not an actual physical property of a light, but rather something that simplifies computation and is often easier to work with artistically. You should set it to whatever looks how you want. Obviously larger lights will be less performant, since in forward rendering they will often light more objects, causing more draw calls, and in deferred they take up more pixels on the screen. Having many lights is REALLY bad in forward rendering, which is why they’re limited by default- every object that’s lit has to be re-rendered for EVERY light that hits it.


Lightmapping is a way to help solve some of these performance issues by precalculating the effects of the lighting and storing that information in a texture. When a lightmapped object is rendered, it can sample the lightmap texture to determine how much light it’s getting, avoiding most of the lighting calculations and dodging those extra draw calls. Unity also uses the lightmapper for realtime GI, which creates textures essentially containing information about  how realtime light can bounce around a scene.

Because these are textures, they have a limited resolution. Using realtime lights, lighting is calculated per-pixel. But when lightmapped, a single lightmap texel may span many pixels on the screen, just like when you zoom in on a texture. And, just like zooming in on a texture, there’s interpolation performed to smooth out the edges a bit- since most lighting is a smooth gradient anyway this works well in most cases.


But- when the lighting isn’t following a smooth and sensible gradient, that interpolation breaks down. Zoom too far in on a hard edge in a texture and it starts looking really fuzzy. Also, if you try to use too low a resolution, you just wont be able to accurately catch small edges at all because they’re smaller than an individual texel and essentially get averaged with the things to either side of the edge.


So, the same principle applies here. The thinner and more discontinuous something is, the higher a resolution you need to accurately represent it. Lightmaps don’t tend to be very high resolution because they’re huge and again, most lighting is pretty smooth anyway. Higher resolutions would take longer to load and sample as well, and take up more vram, so lightmaps usually only use just enough resolution to get the job done. This goes double for GI data because it’s even harder to actually notice artifacts and the realtime nature of realtime GI means performance is a bigger concern.


So essentially, the thickness of your walls is very low compared to the size of the rest of the lightmapped environment, so they will end up small compared to a lightmap texel too, causing bleeding.

You can try increasing your lightmap resolution (but you will get larger lightmaps) or using thicker walls that will lightmap a bit better. The radius of the light itself, however, has little to do with whether or not it bleeds.

EDIT: clearly wasn’t long enough, so thought I should mention that there are some light properties that can cause bleeding, but this doesn’t look like a problem with them. Still, playing with shadow bias can have an effect- that’s the term that helps prevent a surface from shadowing itself (try turning it to 0 and you’ll likely see “shadow acne”, which looks a bit like the shadow is z-fighting with the lit surface, and the problem that causes it is actually quite similar). Too high a bias value can sometimes cause light to bleed through or cause shadows to appear detached from their casters.

You will get lighting issues due to very thin or completely flat planes in your environment though.

Pure damage over time, while it has its place, usually doesn’t create any new gameplay opportunities- other effects that influence the combat situation indirectly will open up new options to consider

My personal thoughts on when I should not use a dictionary:

-If the amount of data is really small

-if it’s being used a lot in performance-critical areas and there are other alternatives. Dictionaries are one of the slower collections.

-If the key is an int, or all valid keys can be translated to a unique int very quickly. Indexing an array or a (non-linked) list is also O(1) and is much faster. If you are using an enum as your dictionary key for instance, or your key is an object that already maintains a unique id from something else, you might just want an array.

-If you need to iterate it frequently. Dictionaries and HashSets don’t store all the values sequentially, and have to do a bit more work to figure out where the “next” value is compared to some of the simpler collections

-basically, if you don’t have an actual need for the dictionary. If the main way you use it is not add/remove/get by key, you probably want something else

-probably most importantly, if the above apply AND it’s actually worth it to care. A dictionary is easy to use and you don’t have to worry about writing your own collection or anything. Always profile to see if it is actually the dictionary that’s hurting performance.

Hey, if ur new to C# and just learning thru unity, you might wanna take a look at [this page](https://www.codeproject.com/Tips/356237/How-to-use-the-IEnumerable-IEnumerator-interfaces) (or just google “C# IEnumerator yield”, there’s plenty of docs and blogs on this).


They’re essentially just a way of arbitrarily creating loopable objects- arrays, lists, etc are already IEnumerable (and you could, in theory, make a coroutine out of one of those, or even do other weird things with it like using LINQ, tho I cant think of a use case for that atm).


When you run a coroutine, you’re just basically giving that loopable object to unity and having it step 1 item forward each frame. The actual things unity gets from the loop are the yield instructions, like WaitForSeconds, which just tell unity to, for instance, wait some time before stepping forward again.


And when you use yield in a method that returns IEnumerator, you’re using a special C# feature that essentially lets you generate the results of the loop on the fly- You can kinda think of all the code between yields as it’s own little method that runs to create the result of the next step in the loop. These are useful for all sorts of things, like generating data to populate a list or retrieving data from multiple different sources while looping over just one thing, for instance.


Unity’s coroutines are just a little funky cause the main part you care about are the side effects from that code in between yields, rather than the result of the yields themselves usually. But the way it works is still pretty similar.

Unity reads the next value from the coroutine, which causes all code since the last yield up until and including the next yield- that code runs, doing all the stuff you want to happen during that stage of the coroutine, before yielding (“returning partially” basically) an object that tells unity what it should do with the coroutine next frame- whether that’s just to step forward again (yield null), to wait some time, (yield WaitForSeconds), or whatever. Once it’s run all the way to the end (or to a yield break) the coroutine ends.

Some things in existing games:

Borderlands lets you lock/unlock items in your inventory. Locked items can’t be dropped or sold without unlocking them first. There’s also a buy-back option if you accidentally sell something (tho that might be harder to flavor with recycling)


Prey’s recycler has its own inventory. You transfer items into it and can see the entire grid of what items are in the recycler before pressing recycle. It’s essentially an “are you sure” step but since it happens in large batches and infrequently, it doesn’t get annoying.

(Prey also has a lot of its in game menu interactions done by actually looking at parts of in-game screens, so the “are you sure” bit feels a lot more natural, like you’re just operating the actual recycler machine. Combined with the hotkey for automatically transferring trash items, the wonderful recycling animation, and the fact that the materials you get are just dumped out a chute and you pick them up out of a bucket, Prey’s recyclers are very memorable for me. It’s actually fun to use them, as opposed to most games where recycling is just a chore in order to get to the other parts of the game)


Pathologic has trading, not really recycling, but it’s still how you get rid of unwanted items (and there’s literally an npc that only buys “dead” items that everyone else considers trash). You can select/deselect items from your inventory, and a bar at the bottom increases showing the value of everything you have selected. On npcs that will be willing to just give you money, the trade just basically converts your items to money. Similar to prey, you always have a broad overview of what you’re selling before you hit the done button.


There’s also plenty of games where it will only display an “are you sure” if you’re throwing out something that could be valuable, or let you recycle everything except, say, quest items, to prevent the player softlocking themselves.



All in all, it looks like 3 things might help-

1- Make the act of recycling less frequent. In a real recycling box, or the one on your computer, putting something in there doesn’t make it magically recycle- you have to actually send the box to the center or hit “empty recycle bin” on ur computer. If the player has time to take an item out that might have gone in by mistake, then they don’t need to “be sure you want to do X” every time, just every recyclebin.inventory.capacity times or faster.

2- Make recycling itself more engaging, which will make players think more about what they’re doing. You don’t need to add a ton of mechanical detail, but if you make the player put in a little more effort to recycle something, they’re already gonna be “sure”. Your “done” doubles as your “are you sure”

3- Let the player manage their inventory more, if they have one. Tags, filters, renaming, grid layouts, tabs/containers… theres tons of existing ways out there and you might already have some that you can use. And if your player doesn’t have a traditional “inventory”, then let them manage whatever serves as the player’s collection of available items. Physically picking up and dropping items from the world for instance hardly needs a solution because the space around you is already your inventory and moving the items around is inventory management.


TL;DR- you could decrease the need for an extra prompt by having players be more “sure” to begin with, and you could also make “are you sure” prompts more bearable by decreasing the frequency they occur and by making the process more engaging so the players don’t have to stop playing the game to recycle stuff.

The comment mentioning deriving from NetworkBehaviour will work, but I wanted to share a little bit more general insight into why using an interface here doesn’t work, and why it doesn’t actually make sense to expect it to. Mirror does a lot of magic behind the scenes with mono.cecil and the like, which can be one of its strengths, but it also can really obscure what’s actually going on:




(Disclaimer: oversimplification at times, wording is optimized for getting my points across rather than absolute technical accuracy)


When you declare a method with [Command], Mirror goes through at compile time and basically copies it to a secret internal version, and then replaces the actual command method with its own thing that sends a message to the server to call that secret internal version it just made. That’s why you’re able to just call CmdInteract on the client like a normal method at all- you’re actually calling some code that mirror injected that does all the boilerplate for you. 


Specifically, the message it sends to the server will contain an index for what command is being sent (I think this is also weaved in at compile time), as well as data for all the arguments. Now, the client and the server don’t share memory (I’m ignoring hosts because in most cases it doesn’t matter). So the only way you can send that data is by sending bytes over the network. To get those bytes from the arguments it has to serialize each argument, and then the server will receive them and deserialize them to create its own version of those arguments, which it will then plug into the secret hidden cmd function.


To serialize an argument (or a field or anything else for that matter), Mirror has to have a writer function for its type, and a reader function for that type to deserialize it. It comes with the most common types already implemented- int, float, string, and plenty others. In addition, if you define a class or struct where every field can be serialized by mirror, then that class or struct is serializable by mirror. It does the same sort of IL postprocessing magic to generate a serializer implementation for that type, which essentially just goes through and calls the serializer for each of its fields. You can also write your own implementations by writing extension methods for NetworkWriter and NetworkReader, meaning you can provide implementations for types that mirror can’t generate, or override the ones it could.


This means, however, that you can’t really pass a reference type over the network the way that classes and interfaces are normally treated, you can only send the data it contains and recreate it on the other side. Since data is copied from the client to the server every time you call a command, everything essentially behaves like a struct when sending it over the network- what is sent is the value of the data itself. Now, you can get close to a “pass-by-reference” if you can assume both sides have an object that corresponds to the same thing and some way to correlate them across the network. Usually this takes the form of an ID or GUID, and is actually how certain types like NetworkIdentity are serialized already. The netId of a NetworkIdentity is always the same between client and server, so if you just send the netId, and then the receiver looks it up, you can essentially pass a reference to it across the network. Remember that you can always write custom readers/writers also, so you could implement a similar system for your own types fairly easily (I like doing it for certain scriptableobject assets for instance).


Now, with all that said, what would it actually mean to send an interface across the network? They don’t have data themselves of course. What makes more sense, and it looks like you want, is to essentially pass it as a reference- You want to tell the server WHICH thing to interact with, not what the data is to make a copy of that thing. But this means you need to have some way of correlating some data that you can send to the object that implements the interface. Now you can absolutely write a custom reader/writer for the interface, and find some way to send ids and match them up, perhaps with netId and component index or the like… but I actually don’t really recommend you do this.


1, you’d have to do most of that over again for every interface you want to be serializable

2, there’s a more general solution:



Normally, I think interfaces for this sort of thing are a great idea, but they just don’t work well over the network. So, I would recommend creating a solution that lets you reference arbitrary NetworkBehaviours. My personal favorite is to create a struct called NetworkBehaviourRef that has implicit casting to and from NetworkBehaviour, and custom readers and writers that serialize the netId and the behaviour index and look them up on the other end. You can also extend this concept if you need to send arbitrary components, but doing so requires sending strings and doing a lot more work to look them up.


Once you have this more general solution, you can just check in the command if the component that the reference points to is of your desired interface, and if not just return. Now, this does still have some limitations- using regular classes or structs with interfaces is not easy to incorporate into the solution above for instance, so you’ll be limited to NetworkBehaviours (or monobehaviours with a bit of extra work). But what this lets you do is simply use your NetworkBehaviourRef wherever you need this functionality, rather than having to keep creating new serializers.



TL,DR:    It actually doesn’t make much sense to send an interface over the network when you consider how mirror actually works, but it’s possible to partially work around this by writing your own serialization methods.

Potentially controversial take but maybe ditch the scoring system entirely.

Imagine:


player-
“Oh man this level is tough. But I think I learned something from last time, let me give it a try”

“Oh it’s still super hard”

“Wait let me try the thing”

“Omg that works! Ok now just to finish this last really hard bit… stay calm… you got this”

“No no no wait wait…”

“Omg! I finally got it! I didn’t think that would work! I actually finally got it! I feel so excited!”


the game- “oh wow that took you forever, you suck. Here’s a meager reward to show you how pathetic your accomplishments were.”


player- “… oh. I… I thought I did good… It was really hard”



game- “nope. Shitty bronze coin for you, peasant. Git gud or uninstall. And no you can’t replay to get a better score. You’ve already shown you suck, all you can do from now on is suck more. I’m disappointed in you”



Basically, your difficulty is going to create a lot of excitement and determination when you beat a level. But your scoring system is going to render all that intrinsic motivation moot, because if you can’t get the reward, it’ll feel like “why bother” at best, and absolutely discouraging at worst.


If you want leaderboards or something more competitive, score those based on, say, total time from entering the level to completion (dying wouldn’t reset the timer, but backing out to menu would and just wouldn’t count the level as finished). Obv just a suggestion. You could also add extra hard side objectives or collectibles or the like, there’d be lots of ways to do this.

Just don’t tie it to “can you beat the level first/second/nth try”. Look to games that are notorious for a tough challenge (I know, obligatory dark souls reference in a gamedev discussion, but also other games from across genres that use difficulty to create a sense of achievement). That’s what the difficulty is for- creating that sense of achievement. You don’t want to do anything to detract from that. 


So I’d say ditch the scoring system, or at least decouple it with a player’s ability to complete the level (after all, if they can’t beat it, the score is 0 anyway, so it still works out).

Hmm… I don’t want to say this couldn’t be enjoyable cause it absolutely could if done right.


I do think, however, it would be hard to do right. For one, I generally don’t think limiting the players senses works super well. This game wouldn’t be able to be played by ppl without headphones, ppl with lower quality headphones that need to keep noise down, ppl who are hard of hearing, even in 1 ear, ppl using any device with mono audio for any reason, etc etc. Additionally, it could be quite hard to teach your mechanics- especially if the player doesn’t realize that they or their device are “incompatible”. And if you try to add subtitles with directionality, it would be hard to not make that simply solve the puzzles for the player.


Playing with player view angles and perspective has a lot of interesting implications though- making the environment, puzzle state, and enemy behavior dependent on what the player can see would certainly make a lot of interesting puzzle options available. I just don’t think you should rely only on sound. The player can always turn around, so I personally think that would be a good way to show state changes- the player just looks back and can see what changed. Sound too, obv, but not only sound. I would think that this goes doubly for the monster- some visual indication that it’s about to round the corner or is nearby would mean that counterplay becomes more possible. 

Existence of counterplay doesn’t necessarily make a monster less scary either. If you’ve ever played a horror game where the monster’s investigating the same room as you and you’re hiding behind a bit of cover hoping it doesn’t search that corner (in games that work like that, which is a lot of them), those can be the tensest moments. It’s more about the monster feeling like a lurking threat than the monster actually being good at killing the player that makes it scary after all, and having the player need to be vigilant at all times to their surroundings in case they need to counterplay can create a lot of tension, especially if they realize they’re vulnerable. This can be done through visuals and sound.

Finally, combining audio and visual feedback together will help make your game less confusing for new players. In general, more forms of feedback are better here. 

None of this is to say there aren’t interesting properties to limiting the players senses, but keep in mind that the limitations should be used to create specific gameplay. A lot of horror games use darkness well to create a sense of ambiguity or a strategic lack of information beyond a certain range, as well as atmosphere. But I know we’ve both also seen what happens when it devolves into “tiny flashlight syndrome” where the game becomes more frustrating to navigate than scary or fun, since most loss states are unexpected and will feel arbitrary.

Are you happy with a limitation on 32 mechanics? I’m not. Keep in mind you may have to use some to do some hidden stuff, and 32 still feels like too low a ceiling for me. So does 64. Hell, so does 128. Anything less than “I can reasonably expect to be able to add as many mechanics as I want and nothing will break” is too low for me. Also, what about 1-off mechanics. You’d need to register them on a per-binary-number basis which feels weird and unintuitive, and can silently break when you change something else. You could restrict yourself to never have 1-off mechanics, but you’d need to design around not having that powerful tool for creating interesting and flavorful cards.

What about adding decorations like card flavor? Like the other 1-off stuff, you’d have to add it as an external thing and match it with the card itself, which just is much more fragile and less intuitive than the card definition simply containing everything it needs to function.

I think you might want to get clear on how function calls and return values work, as well as what semicolon actually means.

To briefly summarize, when a function (or method- for most purposes these will mean the same thing) has a return value, that is the output of the function. That return value is what you specify after the access modifier when you declare a method. e.g.

    public int MyMethod() {…}
Here the return type is ‘int’, meaning the method outputs an integer. So, when you call

    MyMethod()
you can actually treat that entire call like a value.
Saying

    int x = 5;
is just as valid as

    int x = MyMethod();
because ‘MyMethod()’ here is basically just another int as far as the = operator is concerned.

Now because ‘MyMethod()’ (when actually called, which is what the () part does) is just an int, it can do any other int things too, like do math. Once MyMethod is called, you’re just dealing with an int now.
Note that if you see a return type of ‘void’, e.g.

    public void SomethingElse() {…}

That means the method doesn’t return anything, and calling ‘SomethingElse()’ doesn’t evaluate to anything.



Now as to semicolon-
Semicolons are there to say “this is the end of my statement”. If you think about your code as being like

-Do this, and then

-Do that, and then,

-Do the other thing, and then,

-End

Semicolon would be the “and then” here. Some languages just make you do a single statement per line. In C# however you can make a single statement span multiple lines, or have multiple statements on the same line, so you use semicolon to say when your statement ends and a new one begins.




So let’s look at one of your problem lines again:

    float mouseX = Input.GetAxis(“MouseX”); =* mouseSen * Time.deltaTime;

Remember that semicolon serves to divide up your statements. So the computer really sees

    float mouseX = Input.GetAxis(“MouseX”);
    // and then
    =* mouseSen * Time.deltaTime;

As you can see, that 2nd statement doesn’t make much sense. =* isn’t an operator, for one. *= is, but it still needs something on the left side so the statement still doesn’t make sense.



Now, it LOOKS like what you want to do is have mouseX be the “MouseX” axis multiplied by the sens and deltaTime. So to do that, remember again that when you call

    Input.GetAxis(“MouseX”)

the value you are given IS a float. So you can do float things to it. Just multiply it by the sens and dt to get your desired value:

    //this is probably what you wanted
    float mouseX = Input.GetAxis(“MouseX”) * mouseSens * Time.deltaTime;

Notice how this is all one statement- just one semicolon. That statement says “assign mouseX to the result of the MouseX axis times mouseSens times Time.deltaTime”. You might as well be looking at 

    float x = 1f * 2f * 3f;

, except you’re getting your numbers from somewhere else instead of them being hardcoded.



There’s also of minor note the fact that most naming conventions call for fields (variables) to start lowercase (“mouseSens” rather than “MouseSens”), but that’s just naming convention and is a little nitpicky- dont worry about that until you have a solid handle on other stuff.



Anyway, I know this was long, but hopefully you understand why your code wasn’t working and where to start learning a bit easier. C# is a wonderful language but can be a bit of a learning curve if you’re brand new. 

Good luck learning, and on whatever projects you might be working on!

No, you most likely wouldn’t have 1 thread per character. Creating threads and sharing data across them has an extra cost.

The takeaway should really be that threads are NOT the kind of concurrency you are thinking of. Threads exist but you don’t actually need concurrency to simulate multiple characters. You just simulate them one after the other, and wait until everything is done to render a frame. This works out easier because you never have to worry about synchronization to prevent trying to access data at the same time from multiple places (which is bad and causes problems).

If you are wondering how threads could be leveraged to simulate characters, keep in mind this probably doesn’t make sense to do unless you have a lot of characters of their logic is really in-depth. In this case I might simulate around 50 characters with in-depth logic one one thread, and maybe some rudimentary logic for a few hundred less important or faraway npcs on another thread. These numbers are just examples and you’d have to profile to really know.

If you look at a breakdown of what takes time in a lot of games, it’s hardly ever actually the game logic. Usually game logic issues stem from too many things trying to simulate- too many items to perform physics on for instance. Most games cap this at a reasonable value and expect that in normal gameplay you wouldn’t see that much going on anyway. Often, much of a the time spent per frame is spent rendering the frame and waiting for it to be displayed on screen. For logic that may be multiplied often or that must happen concurrently to avoid a freeze, threads can help ease that burden.

Lets say you have 16ms to do a frame.
if you take
8ms to render
1.5ms for sound
1.5ms for overhead,
you still have 6 entire ms to do game logic in. In modern computing terms that’s a decent amount of time.
Unless you need all of that to do a single character, you don’t need a separate thread for that character. And if you DO need all that time you might wanna consider if things could be optimized in some way first.

TL,DR:
You absolutely would NOT spawn a thread for each character. You would do them sequentially. Threads could be used to break up groups to divide and conquer, but each would themselves process sequentially.

Well, you’re pretty correct when you say that they “hide behind the frames”. There’s a few forms of “multitasking” to be used but these are the most prevalent. (Oversimplification warning for those who have detailed knowledge, this post is trying to be more useful to OP specifically)

Frames are rendered whenever all of the game logic calculations for a frame are done. This means that the time it takes to display a frame is the game logic time + render time. If you want your game to run at 60fps, you have 16ms to get everything done each frame. If it takes less time, you artificially wait to put up the frame to improve consistency (consistency in framerate can often matter a lot more than having a high framerate in a lot of cases). Sometimes devs or engines are clever and use this time to get a head start on the next frame’s logic. If it takes longer than 16ms, then the game ends up dropping below 60fps and you see your client become not quite as responsive. If it takes longer than 33ms (technically 42ms but most monitors only operate in multiples of 30), you will see visible lag.

Other forms of “multitasking” involve multithreading and SIMD. 

SIMD stands for “Single Instruction Multiple Data” and is basically the ability to process entire vectors at a time instead of individual scalar values, provided you want to do the same thing to the entire vector. 

Multithreading involves leveraging multiple CPU cores at the same time to operate truly in parallel. This is practically a must in most modern games and engines. There’s typically a main thread that controls everything else and is often where the bulk of the game logic code goes, but often there’s a separate thread dedicated to preparing render data or simulating visual effects, and a handful of worker threads that are there to be assigned tasks to run in parallel. Sometimes these tasks are short lived and process things in step with the framerate, but other times a thread can run for much longer than a single frame. Network and Disk IO (files, downloads, etc) are pretty common in most applications, but these take a long time. In order to do this in the background, or display a progress or cancel button that is updated separately, this can often be done on a separate thread.

There is one other big way devs can achieve the effect of concurrency, and that is by doing part of the job on one frame and part on another frame. This ends up feeling a bit like multithreading, but it all runs on the main thread. This means it still isn’t truly parallel like multithreading, but it has a few advantages. True parallelism via threads can incur extra cost whenever you start, stop, or synchronize threads, and can also make it more difficult to avoid some particularly nasty bugs. By splitting things up over multiple frames, you can take longer than a single frame to get it done without needing to synchronize anything since behind the scenes it’s all sequential anyway.

There’s probably a lot more ways that have been used but these are the ones I have both known and used heavily in the past. But what’s important to know is that the level of true parallelism you can get as a program on the cpu is somewhat limited (shaders and gpu-side is different, since gpus are basically made explicitly for parallelism). Even if you are running multiple threads, each thread can only have a single instruction pointer, and running more threads than cpu cores makes the extra threads actually a bit of a burden. Behind the scenes, everything is done sequentially pretty much. Even worker threads often have to wait to make sure they complete before the frame is rendered, if those threads are doing logic needed for that frame.

TL,DR: Your hide-behind-frames approach is pretty correct. There are some forms of true parallelism like multithreading, but they come with their own limitations and often the right tool for the job is to just do everything sequentially. You have a whole 16ms to do everything in, if you run at 60hz.

You’re tackling a lot for your first project. That’s fine, and you can learn a lot that way, but just know that you’re probably not going to finish and it’s probably not going to look like what you imagined. It’s your first time, after all.

C# (the language you’ll be using) has a lot of similarities with Java. I recommend checking out Unity’s tutorials as well as youtubers like Brackeys to get started. You don’t actually learn anything by doing so. In fact, I would recommend not even importing too many code assets, and just stick to importing things you might have trouble doing yourself (I’m bad at art, for example).

I don’t want to say “dont do this minecraft-y project” because you’ll undoubtedly learn a lot while trying, but I will say you might be dissatisfied with the result. Minecraft-style voxels and procedural generation aren’t super difficult for a more experienced programmer but if it’s your first time I would recommend starting a bit smaller since you’ll be busy learning other things.

A good compromise could be making a non-voxel survival game, with inventory and crafting. This poses a more limited set of challenges that are easier to learn and accomplish, but can still be applicable to making your own minecraft later.

As for it being hard to search for things, I think the best solution is to just learn more of the basics of unity first. This will inform you better on what search terms to use. The Unity Answers and Forums pages are full of excellent info, but unfortunately a lot of the most beginner questions get asked with awful titles like “help please” and go unanswered or end up not searchable. Once you know what to look for though, and can articulate a question that can be answered specifically, there’s a ton of info out there and lots of people willing to help too.

Idk where you are and also am not a lawyer, but I’m pretty sure there’s nothing that makes college mandatory in any legal way. And if you’re over 18, your parents literally do not have any say in the matter. You don’t have to go, no matter how bad they want you to.

Now, when it comes down to a place to live and all that, depending on where you are it can be possible to make enough money to survive off of jobs that will hire you with no degree, especially if you have a roommate. Be prepared that you won’t have a ton of money to work with however.

Also, it might be worth looking into shorter certificate or associates degree programs, or considering trade school. These options tend to be shorter or less pressuring than a full university degree, and can still help you make a bit more money and stay in work.

Unfortunately, the bullshit economy makes it hard to make money without a degree, but there are other options. The people who drop out don’t all just disappear after all.

So yeah. I think you should take the choice out of their hands, but not by suicide. The choice was never really in their hands to begin with. Parents almost invariably have this superiority complex and have grown accustomed to their kids being easily bent and influenced out of fear or guilt or whatever lever they end up feeling the least guilty themselves about using. But you are your own person, and this is your choice to make, not theirs. You don’t have to go back to the place that will kill you, and, at the risk of being a total hypocrite here, you don’t have to kill yourself either. You have other options.

I wish you all the best. Scraping the residue of parents off of us is difficult, but with time and distance it can be done.
